problems.where: S1-O1 (the reconciliation entry for S1-O4 makes the same claim, and S1-O4 measure_detail adds '(Supplementary Materials)')
problems.form_value: Coder identity and reliability are deferred to the Supplementary Materials.
problems.source_says: The paper never names the coders and never reports a reliability statistic. It defers only a detailed description of the AUT scoring to the Supplementary Materials, so whether the supplement holds coder identity or reliability is unknown. The form's own open_questions entry states this correctly.
problems.quote: Elaboration describes how well dyads explained their alternate uses and was scored via coding, with each use receiving 0-2 elaboration points. A detailed description of our AUT scoring is provided in the Supplementary Materials.
problems.locator: p. 7, Section 4.5.1 (repeated in Section 4.5.2). A search of the full PDF text finds no 'rater', 'coder', 'reliability', or 'kappa' outside the reference list.

problems.source_says: The paper gives the size of the comparison: 10 chatbots against 20 human dyads, one score per producer, 30 units in all. The printed U values fit 20 vs 10 (U = 25.0 gives p = 0.001, U = 147.0 gives p = 0.041 with continuity correction). n_units can be 30, not null. The code team fits only the human side, and the other 10 units are chatbots.
problems.quote: In a pre-study to this investigation, we explored how well 10 different generative AI chatbots would perform in the AUT, compared to 20 human dyads.

confirmed: Every S1 outcome is scored by the authors on the AUT answers that dyads or individuals entered: fluency counts uses, flexibility counts categories, originality gives 0-2 points per use by its frequency in the sample, and elaboration is coded 0-2 per use. None is self-reported (p. 7, Section 4.5.1).

AI availability: the AI arm had ChatGPT-4 in the main test (p. 5, Section 4.2.2). In the immediate post-test 'neither condition had access to ChatGPT-4' (p. 6, Section 4.2.3). The retention post-test was done individually 'without ChatGPT-4' (p. 5, Section 4.2; p. 6, Section 4.2.4). So with_ai for S1-O1 to O4 and after_ai for S1-O5 to O12 follow the codebook rule.
S2 uses question 'none', which form-spec.md allows for AI output compared with human output (form-spec.md, field notes, 'question').

Constructs are right: flexibility counts categories within one dyad's own uses, and originality scores the rarity of each use within the cohort, which the codebook codes as novelty. The paper has no across-people similarity measure, so no diversity outcome is missing (p. 7, Section 4.5.1).

Figure 4 prints fluency 14.6 vs 12.7, originality 3.7 vs 3.7, flexibility 10.0 vs 9.4, and elaboration 2.1 vs 3.8, legend 26 vs 26 dyads. All match S1-O1 to O4 (p. 8, Figure 4, checked on the embedded image at full resolution).

Section 5.1.1 prints U = 924.0, p = 0.005 for elaboration and the top-quartile means 23.64 vs 17.77 (sd = 5.08) for fluency and 14.90 vs 12.72 (sd = 1.90) for flexibility, as recorded (p. 8, Section 5.1.1).

Figure 8 prints 16.1 vs 14.4, 3.7 vs 4.0, 11.2 vs 10.7, and 2.8 vs 4.7, legend 26 vs 26 dyads. Section 5.1.2 prints 16.12 (sd = 5.88) vs 14.38 (sd = 4.55) and U = 970.0, p = 0.012. All match S1-O5 to O8 (p. 9, Figure 8 and Section 5.1.2).

Figure 12 prints 7.3 vs 6.8, 2.1 vs 2.0, 6.1 vs 5.7, and 1.9 vs 2.2 with a legend of 26 vs 26 dyads, while Figure 1 shows 52 vs 52 at retention. The values match S1-O9 to O12, and the form flags the conflict (p. 10, Figure 12; p. 5, Figure 1).
Pre-study statistics U = 25.0, p = 0.001 (elaboration, AI better) and U = 147.0, p = 0.041 (originality, humans better) match S2-O1 and S2-O2 (p. 4, Section 4.1).

Unit of S1-O1 to O8: the figure legends say 26 dyads per arm, so team is supported. The U values 924.0 and 970.0 exceed the 676 maximum for 26 vs 26. With 52 vs 52 they give p = 0.0054 and p = 0.013 under the normal approximation, close to the printed 0.005 and 0.012. The form discloses this (pp. 8-9, Figures 4-11 and Sections 5.1.1-5.1.2).

Retention unit participant is supported: RQ3 asks about 'individual participants', and Section 5.1.3 compares 'the individuals of the former experimental groups' (p. 4, Section 3; p. 9, Section 5.1.3).
Primary coding is supported: H1 to H3 name only flexibility and originality, and the authors say they 'formulated and pre-registered hypotheses in advance' (p. 4, Section 3; p. 13, Section 6.4).

Figure 14's Spearman test is labeled dyads, nAI = 26, as the form says, but p = 0.002 for rho = 0.424 fits about 52 rows (n = 26 gives p = 0.031). The doubling the form flags for the U tests seems to apply here too. This is a process measure and changes no outcome field (p. 11, Figure 14).

No outcome is missing: the paper reports four AUT dimensions in three phases, all 12 coded, and the top-quartile variants appear in measure_detail. The other results are process measures (Tables 3 to 5, Figure 14) or self-reports (Section 5.2, Figure 13) (pp. 8-12).
Figure 11's inner title reads 'Main Test: Elaboration Distribution' under an immediate post-test caption, as the form notes (p. 10, Figure 11).
Locators hold: Table 5 is on p. 12, and Section 6.4 runs from p. 13 to p. 14.
summary: Every outcome is scored on the AUT answers by the authors' counts and coding, the question and AI-availability codes follow the codebook and form spec, the constructs are right, and all recorded numbers match Figures 4, 8, and 12 and the text. Two details lack support: S1-O1's measure_detail says the supplement holds coder identity and reliability, which the paper never states, and S2's n_units is null although the paper gives 10 chatbots against 20 dyads.
